rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain early compounds while promoting elution of all 10 within the acquisition window. A moderate gradient duration and midpoint temperature provide a baseline for identifying critical separations and refining the method.
Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing whether the current resolution margin is sufficient. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate gradient compression.

Test temperature-driven selectivity at the faster gradient to separate the crowded middle peaks without restoring the long retention time. This isolates temperature effects and may improve resolution while retaining a negligible time penalty.

Slightly lengthen the gradient at the best-performing temperature to improve the remaining critical separation. The last peak should still elute near 8 minutes, potentially preserving the zero time penalty.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to test a nearby method that may also achieve the maximum CRF. This should improve the 1.59-resolution separation while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes; the other close pair will determine whether full resolution is retained.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test the neighboring higher temperature to assess selectivity around that optimum. This may strengthen the marginal middle-pair separation and shorten retention, although another pair could become limiting.

Return to the optimal temperature and test a slightly higher starting organic fraction as an independent selectivity adjustment. This explores whether maximum CRF can be retained with shorter retention or a stronger minimum-resolution margin.

Reduce the endpoint to slightly flatten injection 7’s gradient, targeting its limiting resolution of 1.29. The observed slope response suggests this could restore full resolution while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes and retaining the maximum CRF.

One further endpoint reduction should raise the limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the other close separation. Extrapolation places the last peak near 8 minutes, making this a candidate for maximum CRF with a better resolution margin.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a distinct low-temperature selectivity regime using the faster gradient. Cooling may separate the crowded middle peaks differently while still allowing the last peak to elute near the zero-penalty time window.

Test the lower-temperature neighbor of the optimal method to bracket its temperature sensitivity. This should improve the earlier critical pair but may weaken the later one, clarifying how narrowly full resolution depends on 55 C.

Use a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9, targeting full resolution with the last peak below 8 minutes. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, so this lower endpoint should preserve the favorable selectivity while offering another maximum-CRF method.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a compensating shallower gradient to seek another maximum-CRF method with improved minimum resolution. The higher start should offset much of the longer gradient’s retention-time increase.

Preserve injection 4’s successful gradient slope while ending the programmed ramp earlier at lower organic content. Since its last peak eluted at 7.60 minutes, before this gradient ends at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, the same maximum-CRF separation is expected.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a substantially faster gradient at 60 C for a possible alternative elution-order regime. The critical pair may separate again after crossing, potentially yielding full resolution at a shorter retention time.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction at 60 C moves the critical middle pair sufficiently beyond its selectivity crossover to recover full resolution. This explores a faster alternative to the established maximum-CRF methods, while checking that the early peaks remain separated.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the early-pair separation seen in injection 16, while steepening the gradient to help keep the middle pair beyond its crossover. This tests another fast alternative; the established CRF of 1.000 remains the campaign maximum.

Keep the optimal initial gradient slope but begin the final hold earlier, after the critical middle peaks have eluted. This tests whether a lower endpoint can preserve maximum CRF; the main risk is delaying the last peak beyond the zero-time-penalty window.

Slightly flatten injection 9’s gradient to improve its earlier critical separation while checking that the later pair remains above 1.5. The last peak should elute around 8.4 minutes, close to the retention time that still incurred no time penalty in injection 18.

Flatten injection 13’s gradient to improve its limiting resolution of 1.10 while retaining its stronger separation of the other close pair. This tests whether a larger minimum-resolution margin is attainable, although the last peak may enter the time-penalty region.

Reduce the endpoint one more step to bring injection 20’s limiting pair above 1.5 while retaining the other close pair’s margin. The predicted last retention time is near 9 minutes, testing whether this better-balanced separation can still achieve zero time penalty.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 21 to increase its limiting resolution toward the other close pair’s margin. This may retain maximum CRF with a more balanced separation, though the later final peak could introduce a time penalty.

Choose a slope between injections 21 and 22 to balance the two critical separations, targeting a minimum resolution near 1.70. The last peak should elute before the gradient ends and slightly earlier than in injection 22, potentially preserving maximum CRF with a stronger resolution margin.
Use a slope between injections 22 and 23 to balance their two limiting separations near R = 1.70. This should retain the maximum CRF while slightly improving the minimum-resolution margin.

Test a slope between injections 21 and 23, expected to retain full resolution with the last peak near 9.1 minutes. This provides a final nearby candidate for the already-achieved maximum CRF, with more resolution margin than the fastest optimal method.
